title: What roles do common CI/CD tools play in a pipeline — SonarQube (static code analysis, coverage, quality gates that fail the build), Trivy/Grype (image & dependency vulnerability scanning), Nexus/Artifactory (artifact/registry repository), and SAST vs DAST (static source scanning vs scanning a running app)?
shortTitle: Roles of Common CI/CD Tools — SonarQube, Trivy/Grype, Nexus/Artifactory, and SAST vs DAST

s1_definition.profdef: These tools each occupy a distinct role in the pipeline. SonarQube performs static code analysis: it inspects source code for bugs, code smells, security hotspots, and measures test coverage, enforcing a quality gate that fails the build if thresholds are not met. Trivy and Grype are vulnerability scanners that check container images and their software dependencies against known-CVE databases and fail the build on severe findings. Nexus and Artifactory are artifact repository managers that store and version build outputs (JARs, container images, npm packages) and act as a trusted internal registry and proxy for external dependencies. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyses source code or bytecode without running it, while DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scans a running application from the outside by sending it real requests.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India's quality controls for a new cheque-processing machine. SonarQube is the design reviewer who reads the blueprints and rejects them if the wiring is messy or untested. Trivy and Grype are the parts inspectors who check that none of the components came from a recalled batch (known vulnerabilities). Nexus or Artifactory is the certified warehouse that stores every approved machine and spare part with a serial number, and is the only place branches are allowed to collect parts from. SAST is reading the blueprint and the parts list before the machine is switched on; DAST is switching the machine on and poking it with test cheques to see how it behaves under real conditions. Together they catch different problems at different stages.
s1_definition.oneliner: SonarQube gates code quality and coverage, Trivy and Grype scan for known vulnerabilities, Nexus and Artifactory store and serve trusted artifacts, and SAST reads the code while DAST attacks the running app.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These tools each occupy a distinct role in the pipeline. SonarQube performs static code analysis: it inspects source code for bugs, code smells, security hotspots, and measures test coverage, enforcing a quality gate that fails the build if thresholds are not met. Trivy and Grype are vulnerability scanners that check container images and their software dependencies against known-CVE databases and fail the build on severe findings. Nexus and Artifactory are artifact repository managers that store and version build outputs (JARs, container images, npm packages) and act as a trusted internal registry and proxy for external dependencies. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyses source code or bytecode without running it, while DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scans a running application from the outside by sending it real requests.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India's quality controls for a new cheque-processing machine. SonarQube is the design reviewer who reads the blueprints and rejects them if the wiring is messy or untested. Trivy and Grype are the parts inspectors who check that none of the components came from a recalled batch (known vulnerabilities). Nexus or Artifactory is the certified warehouse that stores every approved machine and spare part with a serial number, and is the only place branches are allowed to collect parts from. SAST is reading the blueprint and the parts list before the machine is switched on; DAST is switching the machine on and poking it with test cheques to see how it behaves under real conditions. Together they catch different problems at different stages.

**One line to remember:** SonarQube gates code quality and coverage, Trivy and Grype scan for known vulnerabilities, Nexus and Artifactory store and serve trusted artifacts, and SAST reads the code while DAST attacks the running app.

sections.s2_technical:
SonarQube is the code-quality and static-security gate. In the pipeline, after build and test, you run the scanner, for example `mvn sonar:sonar`, which uploads analysis to the SonarQube server. It reports bugs, code smells, duplicated code, and security hotspots, and it ingests the JaCoCo coverage report to know how much of the code tests exercise. The crucial part is the quality gate: a configurable set of conditions such as "coverage on new code at least 80%" and "zero new critical issues." If the gate fails, the pipeline step fails and the change is blocked. For a banking service this stops under-tested or smelly code from progressing.

Trivy and Grype are vulnerability scanners. They take a container image or a dependency manifest and compare every included package and library against public vulnerability databases (CVEs), reporting findings by severity. In the pipeline you run, for example, `trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.2.0`, and the non-zero exit on a high or critical finding fails the build. This catches, for instance, a vulnerable version of a logging library pulled in transitively, before it reaches production. Grype plays the same role with a different engine; teams often standardise on one.

Nexus and Artifactory are artifact repository managers. They serve two purposes. First, they store your own build outputs with immutable versions, so your JAR or container image has a single trusted home and can be promoted across environments by reference. Second, they proxy and cache external repositories like Maven Central or Docker Hub, so builds pull dependencies through your controlled, cached, and policy-enforced registry rather than directly from the internet. This gives reproducibility, speed, and the ability to block banned or vulnerable dependencies at the gateway.

SAST versus DAST is about when and how you look for security flaws. SAST analyses the application without running it, examining source code or bytecode for insecure patterns such as SQL built by string concatenation, hardcoded secrets, or unsafe deserialization. SonarQube's security rules and dedicated tools do SAST, and it runs early in the pipeline on every commit because it only needs the code. DAST runs against a deployed, running instance of the application, sending crafted HTTP requests to find flaws visible only at runtime, such as authentication bypasses, injection that actually reaches the database, or misconfigured headers. Tools like OWASP ZAP do DAST, and it runs later, after the app is deployed to a test environment.

A senior nuance is that these tools are complementary layers, not alternatives. SAST finds issues in your code early and cheaply; vulnerability scanners find issues in your dependencies and base images; DAST finds issues that only appear when the whole system runs together. A bank's pipeline typically runs all of them. Another nuance is managing false positives and gate strictness: an over-strict gate that blocks on low-severity noise trains developers to ignore it, so you tune severities and use suppression with justification for accepted risks. A third nuance is supply-chain integrity: the artifact repository plus scanning plus signing (and generating an SBOM, a software bill of materials) together give provenance, so you can prove what is in a production image and that it came from your trusted pipeline.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India a change to the transfer service shipped with large blocks of untested code, and a null-handling bug reached QA. This is exactly the problem SonarQube's quality gate solves. The gate fails the build when coverage on new code is too low or new critical issues appear, blocking it before QA.

Problem 2 — A vulnerable version of a JSON library was pulled in transitively and ran in production for weeks, which a security audit later flagged. This is exactly the problem Trivy or Grype solves. The image scan fails the build on high or critical CVEs, so the vulnerable library never ships.

Problem 3 — Builds pulled dependencies straight from the public internet, so they were slow, non-reproducible, and occasionally pulled a banned package. This is exactly the problem Nexus or Artifactory solves. All dependencies come through the controlled, cached repository, which also blocks disallowed packages.

Problem 4 — A reflected input-handling flaw was invisible to code review but exploitable on the running API. This is exactly the problem DAST solves, complementing the SAST that already runs on the code.

To make this concrete without the real tools we will write a Java simulation of a security-and-quality gate pipeline. We will model a `QualityGate` (SonarQube) that fails on low coverage or critical issues, a `VulnerabilityScanner` (Trivy/Grype) that fails on high or critical CVEs, an `ArtifactRepository` (Nexus/Artifactory) that stores only artifacts that passed the gates, and a `SecurityScan` with SAST and DAST phases. We will run a change that fails the quality gate, a change that fails the vulnerability scan, and a clean change that passes all gates and is published. This mirrors how the real tools chain together.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -cp target/classes com.bank.tools.CicdToolsDemo

# Real usage (each tool in its stage):
mvn sonar:sonar -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.2.0
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is three builds of the transfer service: A with low coverage, B with critical CVEs, and C which is clean.

Step 1: Build A enters the pipeline. SonarQube reports 55% coverage, which is below the 80% threshold, so the quality gate fails and A is blocked before any later stage runs. Nothing is scanned, nothing is published.

Step 2: Build B enters. Its coverage is 90% and it has no critical issues, so the quality gate passes. Then the vulnerability scanner finds three high or critical CVEs in its dependencies, fails, and blocks B. Again nothing is published.

Step 3: Build C enters. The quality gate passes on 90% coverage with no critical issues. The vulnerability scanner finds no high or critical CVEs and passes. The SAST phase finds no SQL concatenation and passes.

Step 4: Because C cleared code quality, vulnerability scanning, and SAST, it is published to the artifact repository (Nexus), which is the trusted home from which it can be promoted. Only artifacts that passed the gates ever reach the repository.

Step 5: After publishing and a deploy to a test environment, the DAST phase sends requests to the running app, finds no authentication bypass, and passes. Build C has now cleared every static and dynamic gate end to end.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Build artifact
    │
    ▼
  SonarQube (quality gate) ── fail ──→ BLOCKED (coverage/critical)
    │ pass
    ▼
  Trivy/Grype (CVE scan) ──── fail ──→ BLOCKED (high/critical CVE)
    │ pass
    ▼
  SAST (static code) ─────── fail ──→ BLOCKED (SQL concat etc.)
    │ pass
    ▼
  Publish → Nexus/Artifactory (trusted store)   ← only clean artifacts land here
    │
    ▼ deploy to test env
  DAST (running app) ─────── fail ──→ BLOCKED (auth bypass etc.)
    │ pass
    ▼
  Promote to next environment

  SAST = read the code (early)   |   DAST = attack the running app (later)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
These tools each play a distinct, complementary role, and a banking pipeline runs all of them as layers. SonarQube is the code-quality and static-security gate: it analyses source code for bugs, code smells, and security hotspots, ingests the test coverage report, and enforces a quality gate that fails the build if, say, coverage on new code is below eighty percent or there are new critical issues. Trivy and Grype are vulnerability scanners: they compare the container image and every dependency against known-CVE databases and fail the build on high or critical findings, which is how a vulnerable transitive library gets caught before it ships. Nexus and Artifactory are artifact repository managers: they store your own build outputs as immutable versions and proxy external repositories like Maven Central and Docker Hub, so builds are reproducible, cached, and governed by policy.

SAST and DAST are two ways of finding security flaws that find different things. SAST, static application security testing, analyses the source or bytecode without running it, catching patterns like SQL built by string concatenation or hardcoded secrets, and it runs early on every commit because it only needs the code. DAST, dynamic application security testing, runs against a deployed, running instance and sends real crafted requests to find flaws that only appear at runtime, such as an authentication bypass or injection that actually reaches the database, and it runs later after the app is deployed to a test environment.

The reason I run all of them is that they cover different gaps. SAST finds issues in my own code early and cheaply, the vulnerability scanners find issues in my dependencies and base image, and DAST finds issues that only emerge when the whole system runs together. Together with the artifact repository, image signing, and an SBOM, they give provable provenance for what runs in production, which auditors in banking always require.

On the banking project I wired exactly this chain for the transfer service: the SonarQube quality gate blocked under-tested changes, Trivy blocked images with high or critical CVEs, all dependencies resolved through Nexus which also blocked banned packages, SAST ran on every commit, and OWASP ZAP ran DAST against the deployed test instance. The senior point I always add is tuning gate strictness and managing false positives, because an over-strict gate that blocks on low-severity noise just trains developers to ignore it, so I tune severities, require justified suppressions for accepted risks, and keep the gates meaningful enough that a red build is always taken seriously.
